title: GURMEET SINGH versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: GURMEET SINGH v. STATE OF PUNJAB
neutral_facts: The accused, who was married to the deceased, was involved in a dispute over dowry demands. The deceased, who was married within four years of the incident, was subjected to harassment and demands for dowry by her husband. The deceased consumed poison in her matrimonial home, leading to her death. The prosecution presented evidence of the deceased's father, who stated that the deceased had been harassed due to dowry demands. The deceased's mother also informed the father about the harassment.
offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life
physical_harm: deceased consumed poison, leading to her death
number_of_offences: charged under Section 304-B, upheld under Section 304-B
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent and confidence inspiring testimony of deceased’s father (PW4) about continuing harassment meted out to deceased on account of dowry, and the prosecution having satisfied the necessary ingredients u/s.304B IPC
witness_credibility: Both the Trial Court and the High Court found the evidence of P.W.4 to be reliable and consistent despite thorough cross-examination. The testimony of PW4 is found to be consistent and inspiring confidence by this Court as well.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 2008; Trial judgment: 15.03.2010; High Court decision: 15.03.2010; Supreme Court decision: 28.05.2021
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Rishi Malhotra; Counsel for the State: Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Karanvir Gogia, Ms. Shivangi Singhal
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted; High Court: Upheld conviction; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the death of the deceased occurred within seven years of marriage under suspicious circumstances, and there was a proximate and live link between the dowry demand and the death. The accused forged medical records to show a cordial relationship, and the deceased had informed her father about harassment due to dowry demands.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the Courts below applied the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act without satisfying the basic ingredients of Section 304-B, IPC. They claimed the deceased was happy with the appellant, there was no cruelty, and a conviction under Section 304-B could not be sustained without charges under Section 498A.
legal_principle_applied: The Court applied the principle that the prosecution must establish the necessary ingredients of Section 304-B, IPC, and once satisfied, a presumption of causation under Section 113-B, Evidence Act arises, which the accused must rebut.
precedent_relied_upon: Satbir Singh v. State of Haryana 2021 AIR 2627; Kamesh Panjiyar v. State of Bihar [2005] 1 SCR 903; Kans Raj v. State of Punjab, [2000] 3 SCR 662; Rajinder Singh v. State of Punjab, [2015] 2 SCR 835
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution satisfied the necessary ingredients of Section 304-B, IPC, and the accused failed to rebut the presumption of causation under Section 113-B, Evidence Act.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who was married to the deceased, was involved in a dispute over dowry demands. The deceased, who was married within four years of the incident, was subjected to harassment and demands for dowry by her husband. The deceased consumed poison in her matrimonial home, leading to her death. The prosecution presented evidence of the deceased's father, who stated that the deceased had been harassed due to dowry demands. The deceased's mother also informed the father about the harassment. The accused attempted to present evidence of a cordial relationship, including fabricated medical records, which were found to be false by the trial court. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 304-B of the IPC, and the High Court upheld this conviction.

title: RAJ REDDY KALLEM versus THE STATE OF HARYANA & ANR.
case_title: Raj Reddy Kallem v. The State of Haryana & Anr.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.406, s.420, s.120B; Negotiable Instruments Act s.138
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentenced to 2 years of rigorous imprisonment
neutral_facts: The accused entered into a business transaction with the complainant, where the complainant paid an advance amount for the supply of a machine. The accused failed to deliver the machine and issued cheques for the return of the advance money, some of which were dishonoured. The complainant initiated proceedings under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and also filed a complaint under sections 406, 420, and 120B of the IPC. The accused and the complainant reached a settlement in the Lok Adalat, agreeing that if the accused repaid the entire amount, the offences would be compounded or quashed. However, the accused could not meet the payment deadlines, and the settlement was declared frustrated. The accused later paid the full amount and additional interest, but the complainant refused to compound the case. The accused had already been in jail for over a year before being released on bail.
offence_severity: Minimum 6 months to maximum 2 years of rigorous imprisonment
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Multiple offences charged, but the number of offences finally upheld is not stated
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the appellant had compensated the complainant by repaying the entire amount of Rs.1.55 crore and an additional Rs.10 lacs towards interest for delayed payment.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' credibility by noting that the transaction between the parties was purely civil in nature and did not attract criminal law.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant was in jail for more than 1 year before being released on bail and had also compensated the complainant and deposited an additional amount of Rs.10 lacs towards interest for delayed payment.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 2012; Trial judgment: 25.05.2015/29.05.2015; High Court decision: 29.11.2022; Supreme Court decision: 08.08.2023
legal_representation: Ashish Kumar Tiwari, Adv. for the Appellant; Birender Bikram, DAG, Samar Vijay Singh, Keshav Mittal, Ms. Sabarni Som, Fateh Singh, M. K. Dua, Shantanu Sagar, Anil Kumar, Gunjesh Ranjan, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered (FIR No.35 of 2014), charge sheet filed (21.07.2014), trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: conviction and sentence awarded; High Court: impugned order dated 29.11.2022; Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside
prosecution_argument: The State argued that the complainant did not agree to compound the offence, and thus the courts cannot compel the complainant to give consent for compounding. The complainant's unwillingness to compound the case should not be ignored, and the criminal proceedings should continue.
defence_argument: The accused argued that he had fully compensated the complainant and that the criminal proceedings should be quashed as the complainant's unwillingness to compound the case was not a valid reason to continue the proceedings. The accused also emphasized that the transaction was civil in nature and did not attract criminal law.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that while the Negotiable Instruments Act makes offences compoundable, the consent of the complainant is still a necessary condition for compounding. The Court also emphasized that quashing a case is different from compounding and that the court has discretion to quash proceedings if the accused has fully compensated the complainant.
precedent_relied_upon: Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H. [2010] 5 SCR 678 : (2010) 5 SCC 663; K.M Ibrahim v. K.P Mohammed & Anr. [2009] 15 SCR 1300 : (2010) 1 SCC 798; O.P Dholakia v. State of Haryana & Anr. (2000) 1 SCC 762; JIK Industries Limited & Ors. v. Amarlal V. Jamuni & Anr. [2012] 3 SCR 114 : (2012) 3 SCC 255; Meters and Instruments Private Ltd. And Another. v. Kanchan Mehta [2017] 10 SCR 66 : (2018) 1 SCC 560
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant had already been in jail for over a year, had fully compensated the complainant, and had deposited an additional amount of Rs.10 lacs towards interest for delayed payment.
other_sentence_order: The Supreme Court quashed all pending criminal appeals, set aside the conviction and sentence awarded by the trial court, and directed the trial court to hand over the Demand Drafts totalling Rs.30 lacs to the complainant.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused entered into a business transaction with the complainant, where the complainant paid an advance amount for the supply of a machine. The accused failed to deliver the machine and issued cheques for the return of the advance money, some of which were dishonoured. The complainant initiated proceedings under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and also filed a complaint under sections 406, 420, and 120B of the IPC. The accused and the complainant reached a settlement in the Lok Adalat, agreeing that if the accused repaid the entire amount, the offences would be compounded or quashed. However, the accused could not meet the payment deadlines, and the settlement was declared frustrated. The accused later paid the full amount and additional interest, but the complainant refused to compound the case. The accused had already been in jail for over a year before being released on bail. The Supreme Court quashed all pending criminal proceedings against the accused, including the appeals, as the complainant's unwillingness to compound the case did not justify continuing the criminal proceedings.

title: SELVARAJ @ CHINNAPAIYAN versus STATE REPRESENTED BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE
respondent: STATE REPRESENTED BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE
case_title: Selvaraj @ Chinnapaiyan v. State Represented by Inspector of Police
neutral_facts: The accused, a man, was alleged to have caused the death of his 39-day-old daughter. The child was taken to a hospital where she later died. The prosecution claimed the accused strangled the child with a gunny wire and inserted paddy seeds into her mouth. The medical examination did not show signs of strangulation or asphyxia. The autopsy report indicated the child might have died due to sudden death syndrome. Key witnesses, including the mother and maternal relatives of the victim, initially supported the prosecution but later contradicted their statements during cross-examination. The prosecution failed to establish the cause of death as homicidal, and the medical evidence did not confirm the accused's involvement in the child's death.

witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as hostile, with their testimonies requiring scrutiny due to inconsistencies and lack of corroboration.

title: KANCHANBEN PURSHOTTAMBHAI BHANDERI versus STATE OF GUJARAT
case_title: Kanchanben Purshottambhai Bhanderi v. State of Gujarat
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304B, s.498A; Dowry Prohibition Act s.3, s.4
aggravating_circumstances: Demand for dowry, mental and physical harassment
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of accused No.3, convicted of accused No.1 and appellant
high_court_outcome: Acquitted of accused No.1, confirmed conviction of appellant
neutral_facts: The accused, who is the mother-in-law of the deceased, faced allegations of cruelty and demand for dowry. The deceased, a young woman, married into the accused's family and faced harassment and demands for dowry items from the accused and her husband. The deceased confided in her mother and other friends about the harassment. The deceased was found dead after consuming poison, and the post-mortem confirmed poisoning. The prosecution alleged that the accused and her son were responsible for the harassment and dowry demands.
offence_severity: Minimum 6 years, Maximum 7 years RI for Section 304B and 498A IPC
physical_harm: The deceased died of aluminum phosphate poisoning due to torture and harassment
number_of_offences: Three offences charged, two upheld (conviction under Sections 304B and 498A IPC)
premeditation_planning: The court found that the harassment and demand for dowry were specific and proved, indicating premeditation
motive: Demand for dowry and cruelty against the deceased
key_evidence_accepted: The High Court has committed no error in appreciating the evidence for coming to the conclusion that allegations of torture as well as demand of articles by way of dowry against the appellant was clear, specific and stood proved.
witness_credibility: The evidence of material witnesses, particularly informant PW 8, her husband PW 9, a cousin of the deceased PW 10 and a friend of the deceased PW 18, was found to be cogent and specific. The evidence of PW 12, a common relation of both the parties, also disclosed in no uncertain terms the information received from the informant and the deceased's cousin.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 5.7.1998; Trial judgment: 21.01.2009; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: December 05, 2014
legal_representation: Meenakshi Arora, Rahul Narayan, Mohit Singh, Mahima, Vasav Anantharaman for the Appellant; Jesal, Swati Vaibhav, Hemantika Wahi for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal of accused No.3; High Court: Acquittal of accused No.1; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the mother-in-law, appellant, was responsible for the cruelty and demand of dowry against the deceased, which led to her suicide. The evidence of material witnesses proved these allegations, and the High Court correctly convicted the appellant.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant's case stood at par with the acquitted accused, and that the allegations of harassment and dowry demand were general and not specific enough to sustain conviction under Section 304B of the IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that for a conviction under Section 304B of the IPC, it must be proved that the cruelty was in connection with a demand for dowry, and that parity in conviction should be maintained if evidence is common to all accused.
precedent_relied_upon: Satish Chandra and Anr. vs. State of Madhya Pradesh 2014 (6) SCC 723; Durga Prasad vs. State of M.P. 2010 (9) SCC 74; Hardial Singh vs. State of Punjab, 1992 Suppl. (2) SCC 455
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was reduced to seven years RI for offences under Sections 304B and 498A IPC to satisfy the ends of justice, while other sentences remained the same.
other_sentence_order: The bail bond of the appellant was cancelled, and she must surrender or be apprehended to serve out the remaining sentence in accordance with law.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who is the mother-in-law of the deceased, faced allegations of cruelty and demand for dowry. The deceased, a young woman, married into the accused's family and faced harassment and demands for dowry items from the accused and her husband. The deceased confided in her mother and other friends about the harassment. The deceased was found dead after consuming poison, and the post-mortem confirmed poisoning. The prosecution alleged that the accused and her son were responsible for the harassment and dowry demands. The trial court acquitted the father-in-law but convicted the accused and her son. The High Court acquitted the husband but confirmed the conviction of the accused. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of the accused but reduced her sentence.

respondent: STATE REPRESENTED BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE & ORS.
case_title: Postman Vengaisamy & Ors. v. State Represented by Inspector of Police

number_of_offences: 15 accused charged; 15 offences finally upheld

witness_credibility: Some contradictions arose on account of perception of the witnesses and due to passage of time. But the creditability of the witnesses was not shaken. Therefore, such witnesses were reliable and creditworthy.
trial_duration: {'dates_of_offence': 'April 8, 2003 and April 26, 2003', 'trial_judgment': 'December 7, 2007', 'high_court_decision': 'Not stated', 'supreme_court_decision': 'July 24, 2019'}
legal_representation: {'accused': 'P. B. Suresh, Vipin Nair, Karthik Jayashankar, Advs.', 'state': 'M. Yogesh Kanna, Ms. Meha Aggarwal, Partha Sarathi, S. Raja Rajeshwaran, Advs.'}
investigation_status: FIR lodged on April 26, 2003, trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Conviction and sentence', 'high_court': 'Confirmed conviction and sentence', 'supreme_court': 'Appeal dismissed'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that there was a history of previous attack on the complainant party, and on the fateful day, all the accused armed with weapons surrounded PW-1, PW-2 and the deceased. defence_argument: The defence argued that the so-called injured witnesses PW-1 and PW-2 were introduced by the prosecution and their injuries were not proved to be inflicted by the accused. sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the cumulative effect of the evidence led by the prosecution, which established that the accused formed an unlawful assembly with a view to take the life of the deceased, and that the findings recorded by the courts below were plausible findings in law.

title: AMRIK SINGH versus THE STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: Amrik Singh v. The State of Punjab
neutral_facts: The accused were alleged to have committed robbery and murdered the victim during the course of the robbery. The victim and another individual were proceeding from the office of a sub-registrar when three persons on a scooter attempted to stop them. The scooter driver was blinded by red chilli powder and the scooter was snatched. The accused were identified by the victim as the perpetrators. A recovery of Rs.1 lakh from the accused was also presented as evidence. However, the prosecution failed to establish that the victim and the deceased were carrying Rs.5 lakhs in the scooter's dicky, which was alleged to have been looted. The accused were identified by the victim for the first time in court without a test identification parade, which the court found to be a critical flaw in the prosecution's case.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment
physical_harm: Death caused
number_of_offences: Three offences charged, two upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the identification of the accused by PW1 in the Court Room and the recovery of Rs.1 lakh each from the accused as key evidence, but found these insufficient for conviction due to lack of proper procedural compliance.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW1, the eye-witness, as having contradictions in his FIR and deposition, and noted that he did not disclose any description of the accused prior to the trial, which raised doubts about his ability to identify the accused accurately.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 08.05.2001 (post mortem conducted on 08.05.2001), Trial judgment: 01.04.2011, High Court decision: 01.04.2011, Supreme Court decision: 11.07.2022
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Ms. Roohina Dua, Ms. Mansi Gupta, Sangram Saron, Shree Pal Singh; Counsel for the State: Ms. Richa Kapoor, Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Ms. Aishwarya Mishra, Kunal Anand
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Non-conduct of Test Identification Parade (TIP) noted as a procedural lapse
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Sections 302 r/w 34 and 392 IPC; High Court: Confirmed conviction; Supreme Court: Quashed and set aside conviction, acquitted accused
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused were convicted based on the identification of the accused by PW1, the eye-witness, and the recovery of Rs.1 lakh each from the accused, which was alleged to be the looted amount. They also claimed that the complainant and the deceased were carrying Rs.5 lakhs in the dicky of the scooter.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the conviction was solely based on the identification of the accused by PW1 in court for the first time without conducting a Test Identification Parade (TIP), which is a critical flaw. They also contended that the prosecution failed to prove the presence of Rs.5 lakhs in the scooter and that the recovered amount was not the looted amount.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the principle that the identification of the accused for the first time in court without a TIP is not sufficient for conviction, and that the prosecution must establish the connection between the recovered amount and the alleged loot.
precedent_relied_upon: Malkhansingh and Ors. v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2003) 5 SCC 746; Md. Kalam v. State of Rajasthan (2008) 11 SCC 352
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable

title: MANIKANDAN versus STATE BY THE INSPECTOR OF POLICE

case_title: Manikandan v. State by the Inspector of Police
neutral_facts: The prosecution case alleged that the deceased, who was staying with his parents, instructed the accused no.1 to deliver idlis at his home. On the evening of the incident, the deceased came home and asked his mother if the accused had delivered the idlis. Upon learning that the accused had not, the deceased went to the accused's house, where a commotion occurred due to an altercation. The deceased's mother and brother-in-law arrived at the scene. title: BALJINDER KAUR versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: Baljinder Kaur v. State of Punjab
high_court_outcome: Confirmed conviction of the appellant and Pritam Singh
neutral_facts: The accused, Baljinder Kaur, was the sister-in-law of the deceased, Sharanjit Kaur. The deceased married Pritam Singh in January 1997. After two months of marriage, the deceased informed her father and the mediator about the husband and his family members demanding dowry and harassing her. The accused demanded a gold bangle as dowry two months after the marriage. The deceased returned to her father's house due to the dowry demand, but was sent back to her husband's house after one month. She returned to her father's house again with the same demand. Two days before her death, the accused took her back to the matrimonial house. The deceased was found in critical condition and died of poisoning on the way to the hospital. offence_severity: Minimum 6 years, Maximum 10 years
physical_harm: Poisoning leading to death
number_of_offences: Four offences charged, two upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of the father of the deceased (PW-4) regarding the alleged 'dying declaration' and the demand of gold karra by the appellant, but found that the investigation lacked credibility and did not focus on the contents of the complaint.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW-4 (father of the deceased) and PW-5 (Darshan Singh) as providing the main evidence, but noted that their testimony did not establish a proximate live link between the dowry demand and the death of the deceased.
bail_history: The appellant is on bail. The bail bond shall stand discharged.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 25.08.1997; Trial judgment: 11.08.2010; High Court decision: 11.08.2010; Supreme Court decision: 19.11.2014
legal_representation: Dinesh Kumar Garg, Ritu Puri, Advs. for the Appellant; Sanchar Anand, Kuldip Singh, Advs. for the Respondent

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant-Baljinder Kaur demanded a gold karra as dowry two months after the marriage, which led to harassment and cruelty, thereby constituting a dowry death under Section 304B IPC. defence_argument: The defence argued that the demand for a gold karra two months after the marriage was an isolated incident and not 'soon before her death', thus failing to establish the necessary proximity and live link required for a conviction under Section 304B IPC. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the proximity test, emphasizing that for a conviction under Section 304B IPC, there must be a proximate and live link between the cruelty or harassment related to dowry demand and the death of the victim, with the cruelty occurring 'soon before death'.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed under Section 498A IPC, as the evidence on record made out an offence under that section. The appellant had already undergone a period of imprisonment, and the court considered the facts and circumstances of the case.

offence_severity: Minimum: 7 years, Maximum: Life imprisonment

number_of_offences: Multiple offences charged, but only rape (Section 376) and assault (Section 325) were upheld

sentencing_rationale: The court upheld the conviction under Section 376 IPC and imposed a life sentence due to the brutal and grotesque nature of the offence. The death sentence under Section 302 IPC was set aside as the accused was not found liable for the death.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court considered the brutal and grotesque manner in which the offence under Section 376 IPC was committed as an aggravating factor, justifying the imposition of a life sentence.
other_sentence_order: The court modified the sentences, setting aside the death sentence and altering the conviction under Section 302 IPC to Section 325 IPC with a sentence of rigorous imprisonment for seven years. All sentences were to run concurrently.

title: BHAGWANI versus THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
case_title: BHAGWANI v. THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
aggravating_circumstances: Barbaric and savage manner of committing rape and murder on an 11-year-old girl
mitigating_circumstances: Appellant belongs to a Scheduled Tribes community, no criminal antecedents, no adverse conduct in jail

neutral_facts: The accused, along with another individual, attended a ceremony at a house in the evening. The victim, an 11-year-old girl, went missing and was found dead the next morning. The accused and the other individual were present at the ceremony and later visited a local shopkeeper, where they appeared anxious and admitted to having committed a serious act. Their clothes were later seized and examined. Medical evidence indicated the victim was raped and killed. DNA analysis linked the accused and the other individual to the crime scene. The accused had scratch injuries on his body, which were not explained.
offence_severity: Death to life imprisonment for 30 years without remission
physical_harm: Raped and killed an 11-year-old girl
number_of_offences: Charged with multiple offences, conviction upheld for all
key_evidence_accepted: Medical evidence shows that the deceased was raped and killed. DNA profiling of the articles Q, R and S which are the vaginal slide, rectal slide and dried blood on the hair of the deceased showed Y (male) STR. Blood sample of 'S' matched with the articles found on Q, R and S. The Appellant miserably failed to prove an alibi. Importantly, there is lack of any explanation for the scratch injuries found on the body of the Appellant.
witness_credibility: PW-2 (father of victim) along with his family members attended a ceremony at the house of one 'AM' in the evening. His 11 years old daughter went missing and was found dead next morning. PW-4 deposed that he runs a small hotel in the village and the deceased visited his shop to purchase Kurkure at 9.00 p.m. 15 minutes thereafter, the Appellant visited the shop to purchase namkeen. trial_duration: Offence: 14.04.2017; Trial judgment: 03.11.2017; High Court: 09.05.2018; Supreme Court: 2022

investigation_status: Charges framed, final report filed on 27.06.2017, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and death sentence; High Court: Upheld conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Partly allowed, converted death sentence to life imprisonment for 30 years without remission
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the Appellant and 'S' were present at the function at the house of 'AM', and the medical evidence showed that the deceased was raped and killed. The DNA profiling of the articles found on the deceased matched the blood samples of 'S' and the Appellant, and the Appellant failed to prove an alibi. The prosecution also emphasized the gravity of the crime and the need for a severe punishment.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the Appellant was not given a fair opportunity to defend himself, as the trial and sentencing were rushed. They contended that the chain of circumstances was incomplete and not consistent with a single hypothesis proving the Appellant's guilt. They also argued that the death sentence violated the right to fair trial under Article 21 of the Constitution and that mitigating circumstances were not considered.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that death sentence cannot be imposed except in the rarest of rare cases, and that the probability of reformation and rehabilitation of the accused must be considered. precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684; Rajendra Pralhadrao Wasnik v. State of Maharashtra (2019) 12 SCC 460; Mofil Khan and Another v. judicial_aggravating_factors: The Appellant committed the heinous crimes of kidnapping, rape, and murder of an 11-year-old girl in a barbaric and savage manner.
other_sentence_order: The conviction under Sections 363, 366A, 364, 346, 376D, 376A, 302, 201 of IPC and Section 5(g)(m) read with Section 6 of the POCSO Act was upheld, and the sentence was converted from death to life imprisonment for 30 years without remission.

title: VADLAKONDA LENIN versus STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the death penalty should be imposed only in the 'rarest of rare' cases, where the sentence of life imprisonment is foreclosed and the aggravating circumstances outweigh the mitigating ones.

sentencing_rationale: The death sentence was imposed due to the heinous nature of the crime, the cold-blooded murder of two children, and the lack of remorse shown by the appellant. The court considered the crime to be in the 'rarest of rare' category.

title: AMIT versus STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH

mitigating_circumstances: Appellant was young, no prior criminal record, potential for reform

neutral_facts: The accused, a neighbor, took a three-year-old girl from her home on the pretext of giving her biscuits. The girl was later found dead in a field. witness_credibility: PW-3, the grandmother of the victim, was not an interested witness. Her evidence was not disbelieved despite her age and partial vision, as she could fully see and identify the appellant.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant did not reply when asked about the whereabouts of the victim and ran away. He was apprehended after the victim's body was recovered.

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that a near relative of the victim is not necessarily an interested witness, and that the death sentence should be converted to life imprisonment for a young offender who may reform and is not likely to repeat crimes.

The trial court applied the provisions of Section 113-B of the Evidence Act, which presumes that dowry demands were involved in such cases. The victim died within two months of her marriage. The accused was present at the scene of the incident, and the victim also mentioned that her sister-in-law was present but did not make any allegations against the accused.

title: RAM SINGH @ CHHAJU versus STATE OF H.P.
case_title: RAM SINGH @ CHHAJU v. STATE OF H.P.
neutral_facts: The accused, a man in his early twenties, allegedly committed rape on a woman in her early forties. The victim, a midwife, was approached by the accused at her home, where she was staying with her husband and son. The accused persuaded her to accompany him to his house to assist with a delivery. During the journey, the accused and another man forcibly raped the victim. The victim later reported the incident to the police, and medical examinations indicated that the rape occurred approximately 12 to 14 hours prior to the examination.

number_of_offences: Charged with one offence under Section 376 IPC; upheld by the High Court
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of victim corroborated by witnesses as also by medical evidence; at the site of incident, grass and plants found damaged and ruffled; absence of injuries on the person of victim and her private parts not fatal to the prosecution case; failure of investigating officer to send blood stained clothes of victim for investigation would not discredit the testimony of victim.
witness_credibility: The testimony of the victim inspires confidence. Her testimony is not only corroborated by other witnesses but also by the medical evidence. defence_argument: The defence argued that the trial court's acquittal was correct, as the prosecution failed to prove the incident with reliable and independent evidence, and the victim's testimony lacked corroboration.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the absence of defence injuries does not necessarily invalidate the prosecution's case, and that an appellate court has the power to re-appreciate evidence and overturn an acquittal if it finds the trial court's findings perverse.

neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a man in his early twenties, allegedly committed rape on a woman in her early forties. During the journey, the accused and another man forcibly raped the victim. title: BIRENDRA DAS & ANR. versus STATE OF ASSAM

title: NEERAJ SHARMA versus STATE OF CHHATTISGARH
case_title: Neeraj Sharma v. State of Chhattisgarh
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of offences under sections 307/120B, 364A and 392/397 IPC
neutral_facts: The accused, Neeraj Sharma and Ashwani Kumar Yadav, abducted the victim, Arjit Sharma, while he was staying as a paying guest in the house of Seema Singh. The victim was taken on a motorcycle ride and during the journey, the accused attempted to strangle him with the clutch wire of the motorcycle. The victim fell unconscious and the accused believed he was dead, so they poured petrol on his body and set him on fire. The victim survived and sustained severe burn injuries, which resulted in the amputation of his right leg. The victim was later rescued and taken to the hospital. The prosecution established the abduction and attempt to murder, but failed to prove the demand of ransom necessary for the offence under section 364A IPC. witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, particularly the complainant, as credible despite his injuries and the traumatic nature of the incident. title: NAND KISHORE versus STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
case_title: NAND KISHORE v. STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.363, s.366 and s.376(2)(i); Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 s.354(3)
neutral_facts: The accused, a manhole worker, was involved in the rape and murder of a minor girl. The victim, a minor girl, went to a 'Mela' with her younger brother. The accused took the victim away from the 'Mela' and committed rape and murder. The victim's brother identified the accused in a test identification parade and stated that the accused took the victim away. A witness reported seeing a dog with a child's leg, and the victim's headless body was found in bushes. Forensic and medical evidence indicated severe injuries on the victim's private parts. The accused's blood-stained clothes and items used for the offence were recovered from his house. The case rested on circumstantial evidence, with the 'last seen' theory applied to the facts.

physical_harm: Severe injuries including fractured legs and internal injuries leading to death
number_of_offences: Charged with 4 offences, 4 upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the circumstantial evidence, including the 'last seen' theory, forensic and medical evidence, and the identification of the accused by PW-4 and PW-7.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, including PW-4 (brother of the deceased) and PW-7, as reliable and their statements were considered along with forensic and medical evidence.

The evidence included the testimony of PW-4, the brother of the deceased, who identified the accused in the Test Identification Parade and stated that the appellant took away the deceased. PW-1 reported seeing a dog with a child's leg, and the headless body of the deceased was found in the bushes. The prosecution also highlighted the forensic and medical evidence, including severe injuries on the private parts of the deceased and the recovery of blood-stained clothes from the appellant's house.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, as the case rested solely on circumstantial evidence. The appellant claimed he was denied proper legal assistance and is a manhole worker. The defence also submitted that the trial court and High Court did not consider relevant mitigating circumstances and that the death sentence was imposed without examining special reasons under Section 354(3) of the Cr.P.C. The appellant also pointed out that the local Bar Association refused to represent him, leading to inadequate legal representation.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the 'last seen' theory and the test of the 'rarest of rare' cases, emphasizing the need to consider mitigating circumstances and the legislative policy under Sections 235(2) and 354(3) of the Cr.P.C. The Court also referred to the ratio laid down in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and other precedents to determine the appropriateness of the death sentence.
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684; Swamy Shradhananda(2) v. State of Karnataka (2008) 13 SCC 767; Neel Kumar v. State of Haryana (2012) 5 SCC 766; Selvam v. sentencing_rationale: The death sentence was modified to life imprisonment with an actual period of 25 years, without any benefit of remission, as the case did not fall within the 'rarest of rare' category. The Court found that the reasons assigned by the trial court and High Court did not constitute special reasons under Section 354(3) of the Cr.P.C. to impose the death penalty.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The Court considered the appellant's age (about 50 years), his occupation as a manhole worker, and the lack of finding that there was no possibility of reformation. The Court also noted that the appellant was not adequately represented by legal counsel during the trial.
other_sentence_order: Sentences imposed for all offences to run concurrently. The appellant is to serve life imprisonment with an actual period of 25 years, without any benefit of remission.

title: STATE OF MAHARASHTRA versus ABU SALEM ABDUL KAYYAM ANSARI AND ORS.

neutral_facts: The case involves a murder committed by a group of individuals, with the victim being Pradeep Jain. The accused, including Abu Salem Abdul Kayyum Ansari, were involved in a conspiracy to murder the victim. The accused were tried for the murder, and the trial involved an accomplice who was granted conditional pardon under Section 307 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The accomplice was later found to have breached the conditions of his pardon, leading to a dispute over whether he could be cross-examined by the co-accused.
offence_severity: 302, 307, 120B, 23, 114 IPC, Sections 3, 25(1B)(a), 5, 27 of the Arms Act and Sections 3(2)(i), 3(2(ii), 3(3), 3(5), 5, 6 of TADA Act
physical_harm: Injuries or death caused, briefly
number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged and how many were finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The court accepted that the approver, Riyaz Ahmed Siddique, had been granted conditional pardon under Section 307 Cr.P.C. for making full and true disclosure of the facts concerning the murder of Pradeep Jain. However, upon the Public Prosecutor issuing a certificate under Section 308 Cr.P.C. that he had not complied with the condition, the court held that he was reverted to the position of an accused and his evidence was rendered useless for the trial of the co-accused.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the approver, once his pardon was forfeited, was relegated to the position of an accused and thus his evidence was not considered credible for the purposes of the trial of the co-accused. The court also noted that the evidence of an accomplice is generally unworthy of credit unless corroborated, as per Section 114 of the Evidence Act.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: March 7, 1995; Trial judgment: July 11, 2001; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: October 5, 2010

defence_argument: The defence argued that the withdrawal of pardon by the public prosecutor did not automatically strip the approver of his status as a witness. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that once an accomplice is granted pardon under Sections 306 or 307 Cr.P.C., he becomes a witness for the prosecution. prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused and the victim were working together in a business, checked into a hotel together, and that the accused locked the hotel room and left with the key, leading to the victim's death. The prosecution also relied on the room boy's testimony and the manager's statement about the decomposed body found in the room.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the accused should be given the benefit of the doubt, and that the witnesses (room boy and manager) had access to the room and motive to commit the crime, making their statements unreliable.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the prosecution must prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and that the accused is not required to establish their innocence. The court also emphasized the importance of proper investigation and the need for identification parades in capital cases.
precedent_relied_upon: Parsuram Pandey vs. State of Bihar 2004 (5) Suppl. SCR 475; Arsaf Ali VS. State of Assam 2008 (10) SCR 1115; Sher Singh vs. State of Haryana (2015) 1 SCR 29

judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered that the accused surrendered after one and a half years without any outstanding warrants, and that there was no explanation for why the police did not arrest him despite frequenting his home.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and the victim were working together in a business. They checked in at a hotel on the same day. The accused locked the hotel room and left alone with the room key and did not return. Two days later, a room boy noticed a bad odor coming from the room. The room was opened the next day with a master key given by the manager, and the decomposed body of the victim was found in the room. Eighteen months later, the accused surrendered before the judicial magistrate. The accused allegedly voluntarily confessed to killing the victim, but in his statement under s.313 CrPC, he denied his complicity in the offence. The courts below convicted and sentenced the accused under s.302 IPC based on circumstantial evidence. The High Court was not correct in drawing an adverse inference against the accused because of what he stated or failed to state under s.313 CrPC. The investigation conducted by the police was not satisfactory. Both the prosecution and the High Court took the deposition of the room boy to be trustworthy, ignoring the fact that the room boy and the manager had access to the hotel room for three days before the body of the deceased was found. They had as much motive and opportunity to commit the crime as was attributed to the accused. The statement of these witnesses cannot be relied upon. The failure of the prosecution to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt led to the accused being given the benefit of the doubt.

title: SHAHID ALI versus THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH

witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as hostile, with many of them turning against the prosecution during cross-examination. The credibility of the witnesses was undermined as they provided conflicting accounts and were found to be based on hearsay.

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the Appellant shot the deceased during a marriage ceremony, resulting in his demise, and that the Appellant was guilty of the offence under Section 302 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no previous enmity between the deceased and the Appellant, no intention to cause death, and that the act of celebratory firing during a marriage ceremony should not be construed as an act so imminently dangerous to cause death.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that an act is punishable under Section 304 Part II IPC if it is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, even if there is no intention to cause death.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the Appellant's act of celebratory firing in a crowded place without taking safety measures led to the death of the deceased, and the Appellant was found guilty of culpable homicide under Section 304 Part II IPC.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the absence of previous enmity, the lack of intention to cause death, and the fact that the Appellant had already undergone approximately 8 years of incarceration.
other_sentence_order: The conviction and sentence under Sections 25 & 27 of the Arms Act remain unaltered. The Appellant is to be released forthwith if not required in any other case.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused was present at a marriage ceremony and fired a weapon, resulting in the victim's death. The victim was shot in the neck, leading to his demise on the spot. An FIR was registered under Section 302 IPC, and a confession was obtained from the accused under Section 161 CrPC. A separate FIR was registered under Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts, a post-mortem report, and an inquest report. However, all eyewitnesses turned hostile during the trial, and the trial court convicted the accused under Section 302 IPC. The High Court upheld this conviction. The Supreme Court re-examined the case, focusing on whether the act of celebratory firing could be considered an act so dangerous as to cause death. The Court noted that there was no prior enmity and no evidence that the accused aimed at the victim. The accused was found guilty of culpable homicide under Section 304 Part II IPC, and the conviction under Section 302 IPC was set aside.
